sysd-q-115.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
sysd-q-115.text: SMTP only pushes mail; it never pulls it. The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol is the Internet standard that mail servers and clients use to transmit electronic mail, and it is a delivery protocol only. Mail goes to the next-hop server as it arrives, routed by destination server rather than by individual user, while POP and IMAP handle retrieval. SMTP is connection-oriented and text-based: a sender issues command strings and a receiver replies, over a reliable ordered stream, typically a TCP connection. Replies are 2xx positive, 4xx transient or 5xx permanent. Servers talk to each other on TCP port 25, and clients submit mail on port 465 or 587 to a submission server that requires authentication. Original SMTP could not authenticate senders, so spoofing is possible. Modern servers add SPF, DKIM, DMARC, DNSBLs and greylisting to reject or quarantine suspicious mail.

sysd-q-136.title: Email message format
sysd-q-136.text: An email message is plain text, and one blank line splits it in two. It is a header section of fields followed by an optional body, in the syntax RFC 5322 specifies, and a blank line separates the two. A header field is a name, a colon and a field body. A long body can be folded onto several lines by inserting a line break before whitespace. A conformant message uses US-ASCII characters, with each line at most 998 characters and ideally at most 78. The header fields carry most of the semantic information, because the RFC 5322 body is only a series of uninterpreted lines of text. Non-ASCII header text uses the RFC 2047 encoded-word syntax, and non-ASCII bodies use the encodings of {{ref:sysd-q-123}}. A header must include at least a From field and a Date field.

sysd-q-123.title: MIME
sysd-q-123.text: Email was designed for 7-bit ASCII, so how does a photo get through? MIME, the Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, extends the email format to carry non-ASCII text and multimedia attachments. It adds character set specifiers and two content transfer encodings: quoted printable for mostly 7-bit text, and base64 for arbitrary binary data. Attachments are widely sent as base64 because original SMTP transports only 7-bit ASCII, so the attachment is encoded before sending and decoded on receipt. A MIME message can hold several parts. The type multipart/mixed carries a cover letter and documents, multipart/alternative the same content in several formats, and multipart/related HTML with its images. Parts can nest, and the sender can mark a part as shown inline or as an attachment. The message forms a tree whose leaves are single-part content types and whose inner nodes are multipart types, which lets IMAP fetch one part without the rest.

sysd-q-128.title: Email spam
sysd-q-128.text: Most email is junk. Email spam is unsolicited messages sent in bulk by email. Because sending is cheap, it grew to an estimated 90% of global email traffic by 2014 and about 85% of email in 2021. Spam burdens recipients, who must manage, filter or delete it without compensation from the sender, which makes it a negative externality. Spammers need addresses, so they and list merchants gather huge lists, harvesting addresses without the owners' consent. They misspell filtered words or hide the message text in an image to defeat pattern-matching and text-based filters. They send through vulnerable third-party systems such as open mail relays, open proxies and networks of malware-infected PCs, called zombies. To resist, administrators pre-emptively block dynamic IP ranges, require forward-confirmed reverse DNS and impose strict requirements on delivering servers, which can burden small domestic mail servers. Many ISPs block outgoing port 25.

sysd-q-130.title: SMTP mail transaction
sysd-q-130.text: An SMTP conversation is strictly polite: one command at a time. A mail transaction hands one message to a server in three steps: MAIL, one or more RCPT, then DATA. A session starts when the client opens a connection and the server sends a greeting. The client then normally sends EHLO to identify itself, and the dialog stays lock-step unless pipelining is agreed. MAIL starts a transaction and resets the receiver's state. Its reverse-path is the source mailbox used to report errors, and a 250 reply accepts it. RCPT gives one forward-path per command and can be repeated. A recipient known to be undeliverable gets a 550 reply, and RCPT without a prior MAIL gets 503. After DATA the server replies 354 and treats the following lines as the message until a line holding only a period. The client must not send message data unless it gets 354. To let users send a line that is a single period, the client adds an extra leading period to any line starting with one. The server removes it. When the server finishes storing the data it sends 250, which confirms the transaction. By returning 2yz, the server accepts responsibility to deliver the message, retry transient failures and notify the sender of permanent ones. A 4yz after the end of data means the server must not deliver and the client keeps responsibility. A 5yz means the client should not retry to the same server without review. The client ends the connection with QUIT, to which the receiver must send 221 before closing.

sysd-q-134.title: SMTP envelope versus message header
sysd-q-134.text: A letter's address is written on the envelope, not on the page inside, and email works the same way. A mail object has an envelope that SMTP uses for delivery and content made of a header section and a body. The envelope holds the originator address to which errors are reported, one or more recipient addresses and optional extension data. The content, sent in DATA, has a header section and a body. Delivery follows the envelope, not the header. So the To field may be unrelated to the addresses the message is delivered to, and From may not be the actual sender. Bcc recipients are normally given only in the envelope and not listed in the header. Return-Path, added at final delivery, preserves the MAIL command's reverse-path, which can differ from the sender's mailbox when errors go to a special error-handling mailbox. The content is US-ASCII text, though extensions such as 8BITMIME can relax the restriction for the body.

sysd-q-137.title: Email header fields
sysd-q-137.text: Header fields come in six groups. Originator fields say who sent the message. From names the author, and Sender names the agent that actually transmitted it and must appear when From has several mailboxes. Reply-To suggests where replies go, or else they go to From. Destination fields name the recipients: To holds the primary recipients, Cc others who receive a copy, and Bcc recipients whose addresses are not revealed to the others. How Bcc is handled is implementation dependent. The line may be removed from every copy, or Bcc recipients may get a separate copy that carries it. Identification fields matter for conversations: every message should have a Message-ID, and replies should carry In-Reply-To and References. Informational fields are Subject, Comments and Keywords, optional and meant for humans, and Subject is the most common. Trace fields record the route. Each SMTP server prepends a Received line and must not change or delete earlier ones, and final delivery adds Return-Path, so the timestamps help find slow relays. Servers can also record authentication checks in fields such as Authentication-Results, Received-SPF and DKIM-Signature. Resent fields are added when a user reintroduces a message into the transport system; they are informational and must not drive normal reply handling.

sysd-q-132.title: SMTP queueing and retries
sysd-q-132.text: Email expects some deliveries to fail at first, so it keeps trying. Mail that cannot be transmitted immediately must be queued and periodically retried, and a queue entry holds the envelope information as well as the message. After a failed attempt the sender must delay retrying that destination. The retry interval should be at least 30 minutes, and the give-up time generally at least 4-5 days. Failures are typically transient. That favors two connection attempts in the first hour, then backing off to one every two or three hours, in the spirit of {{ref:sysd-reliab-079}}. A client should keep a list of unreachable hosts with their timeouts rather than retry every queued item. Retrying many messages to a dead host wastes overhead and blocks the sender. When several recipients share a destination server, only one copy should be sent: one MAIL, a RCPT for each recipient, then one DATA. Retry parameters must be configurable, and every activity needs a per-command timeout.

sysd-q-133.title: Bounce messages
sysd-q-133.text: A server that accepts a message with 250 after DATA takes on responsibility for it. It must not lose the message for frivolous reasons such as a later host crash. A bounce message is the notice an SMTP server sends the originator when it accepted a message but cannot deliver it. The notice goes to the envelope return path, using a null reverse-path (<>) for the notice itself. Servers must not send notifications about problems with notifications, so no notice is sent when the return path is already null, and the null path prevents error-report loops. Some failures after acceptance cannot be avoided. A soft DNS error may block recipient validation, the target may be a mailing list, or the server may be a relay. Rejecting a message during the SMTP transaction is better than bouncing it afterwards. Backscatter happens when a misconfigured server bounces mail whose envelope sender was forged, so the bounce lands on an innocent party. Many ISPs disable non-delivery reports for this reason.

sysd-q-116.title: Mail agents and relays
sysd-q-116.text: A message crosses several programs between its sender and its reader. A mail user agent submits mail to a mail submission agent, which hands it to a mail transfer agent (MTA). The submission and transfer agents are often the same software started with different options. The boundary MTA looks up the recipient domain's mail server in DNS, using the record described in {{ref:sysd-q-126}}, and connects to the target MTA. Transfer is one connection between two MTAs or a series of hops through intermediaries. A receiving server may be the final destination, a relay that stores and forwards, or a gateway that forwards using a protocol other than SMTP. A relay passes on the message data without modification except for adding trace information. A gateway may need to transform the message because the two transport environments differ. Counting the Received header fields is an effective way to detect mail loops, with a large rejection threshold, normally at least 100 entries. The final hop hands the message to a mail delivery agent, which saves it in the mailbox format or forwards it by SMTP or LMTP. Clients then retrieve mail with IMAP or POP. A relay returns 550 if policy forbids relaying.

sysd-q-126.title: MX record
sysd-q-126.text: How does a sending server know where to deliver mail for a domain? It asks DNS for an MX record, a DNS resource record naming the mail server responsible for accepting email on behalf of that domain. An MX record carries a preference value and the host name of a mail server, and a domain may have several of them. The sending MTA gets the list of servers with their preferences and tries the lowest preference number first. The preference is an unsigned 16-bit field, so valid values range from 0 to 65535. The named host must map to address records (A or AAAA) and must not point to a CNAME record. With no MX record, the sender treats the domain as having an implicit MX of preference 0 pointing at itself. A temporary DNS error means the message must be queued and retried later. Several MX records give load balancing and redundancy, and allow high-availability clusters of mail gateways for one domain. They cannot move mail service to another port or weight servers of unequal priority.

sysd-q-120.title: Post Office Protocol
sysd-q-120.text: POP is built to empty the mailbox. The Post Office Protocol is an application-layer Internet standard protocol that email clients use to retrieve email from a mail server. It gives a client access to a mailbox, called a maildrop, and supports list, retrieve and delete operations on messages. POP3 clients typically connect, retrieve all messages, store them on the client computer and delete them from the server. This suited users with only temporary dial-up connections who read mail offline. Clients may instead leave mail on the server and download only new messages, identified through the UIDL unique-id list command. Mail marked for deletion is removed from the maildrop only when the client ends the session. A POP3 server listens on TCP port 110, and encryption is requested with the STLS command or by connecting to POP3S on port 995. The original login was an unencrypted USER/PASS pair, and APOP adds a challenge-response using MD5.

sysd-q-122.title: Email delivery
sysd-q-122.text: Email travels from the sender's mail client to the recipient's mailbox in a handful of hops. The sender's mail user agent formats the message and sends it with the submission protocol, a profile of SMTP, to its local mail submission agent. That agent takes the destination from the SMTP envelope, not the message header. The part before the @ is the local part, and the part after is a domain name it resolves in DNS. DNS answers with the MX records listing the domain's mail exchange servers, which are MTAs, often run by the recipient's ISP. The sending server transfers the message by SMTP. The receiving MTA may forward it to other MTAs before the mail delivery agent places it in the recipient's mailbox. The recipient's client then collects it by POP3 or IMAP. Domains usually have several mail exchange servers so they can keep accepting mail when the primary is unavailable. Email favors reliability over speed to cope with unreliable links and busy servers. Mail can be queued and retried for up to five days before a permanent-failure notice. Accepting a message obliges an MTA to deliver it or send a bounce message back. Open relays that accepted mail for anyone were exploited by spammers, so they are now rare and many MTAs refuse mail from them.

sysd-q-119.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
sysd-q-119.text: IMAP makes a remote mailbox behave like a local folder. It is an Internet standard protocol that email clients use to retrieve and manage messages on a mail server over a TCP/IP connection. It was designed for complete management of a mailbox by multiple clients. Clients generally leave messages on the server until the user deletes them. The server holds the mailbox structure of content, folders and per-message state, and local copies are only a temporary cache. So IMAP needs far more server resources and cost per mailbox than POP. Flags such as read, replied to or deleted are stored on the server, so different clients see each other's changes. Clients can ask the server to search, and can fetch individual MIME parts such as the text without its attachments. IMAP IDLE lets the server notify connected clients of mailbox changes, but clients must keep a TCP connection open. An IMAP server listens on port 143, or 993 for IMAP over TLS, and RFC 9051 defines the current version.

sysd-q-121.title: POP versus IMAP
sysd-q-121.text: POP downloads, and IMAP shares. POP downloads mail to one device, whereas IMAP keeps the mailbox on the server so many clients can share it. POP3 moves messages from the server to the client and deletes them there, though it can leave them. POP gives a completely static view, so the client must reconnect and re-authenticate to see changes. IMAP gives a dynamic view and reports new mail and changes made by other connected clients. POP has no folders and no server-side message state, so two POP clients cannot sync read state. It has no IDLE either, so clients must reconnect periodically to check. POP is simpler and easier to implement. IMAP remedies many of its shortcomings, at the cost of far more server resources per mailbox. A POP UIDL is a visible ASCII string up to 70 characters, while an IMAP UID is a number local to a folder, paired with a UIDVALIDITY value. Webmail providers such as Gmail and Outlook.com support both.

sysd-q-143.title: IMAP commands and responses
sysd-q-143.text: An IMAP session is a text dialogue in which the client sends tagged commands and the server returns data and a tagged completion result. IMAP assumes a reliable data stream such as TCP and listens on port 143, or 993 for implicit TLS. Each client command carries a tag. The server's completion response repeats it with OK, NO or BAD, a protocol error, so the tag shows which command finished when several are in progress. Server data and other status lines start with "*" as untagged responses and may be sent unilaterally. A client must therefore be ready to accept any response at any time. A client may pipeline commands without waiting for completion. If a command could affect another's results, the server must execute them in the order given. The server must send mailbox size updates automatically, and only EXPUNGE may reduce the message count, because EXISTS cannot. A connection is in one of four states: not authenticated, authenticated, selected or logout. A client must select a mailbox before commands that affect messages.

sysd-q-140.title: IMAP unique identifiers
sysd-q-140.text: How does an email client tell messages apart when it returns a week later? An IMAP unique identifier (UID) is a number that identifies a message in a mailbox, stable across sessions when paired with the mailbox's UIDVALIDITY. A message can also be addressed by its sequence number, its relative position from 1 to the number of messages in the mailbox. A UID is an unsigned non-zero 32-bit value assigned in strictly ascending order as messages are added, and it need not be contiguous, unlike a sequence number. A UID must not change during a session and should not change between sessions, so an offline client can resynchronize. UIDVALIDITY lets a client detect changed UIDs: if UIDs fail to persist, the new value must be greater than the old. UIDNEXT is the predicted UID of the next new message, so a client can tell whether mail arrived since it last checked. The mailbox name, UIDVALIDITY and UID together must refer to a single immutable message forever, and an expunged message's UID is never reused under the same UIDVALIDITY.

sysd-q-125.title: Email spoofing
sysd-q-125.text: Original SMTP could not check who a sender really was. Email spoofing is designing a message's header so it appears to come from a known or trusted source. Spam and phishing typically use it to mislead the recipient about the message's true origin. Even casual users can negotiate directly with receiving and relaying servers to build a misleading message. A sender's own software can set From freely. A domain owner can specify which servers may send for the domain, and servers can sign mail with SPF and DKIM, so spoofed addresses can be flagged. These techniques do not protect against misspelled lookalike domain names.

sysd-q-118.title: SMTP security
sysd-q-118.text: SMTP cannot authenticate mail or check integrity at the transport level, so its security is built around it. That means authenticating clients, encrypting server-to-server connections and declaring a domain's TLS policy. SMTP-AUTH makes the client log in to the mail server, which lets legitimate users relay mail and denies relay to spammers. It does not guarantee the authenticity of the envelope sender or the From header. Spoofing remains possible unless the server limits from-addresses to those the user may use. STARTTLS lets a server advertise TLS and a client upgrade the connection. It is opportunistic and resists only passive observation, because negotiation is in plain text and an active attacker can strip the commands, a downgrade known as STRIPTLS. MTA-STS lets a domain declare, in a policy file and DNS TXT record, that it supports secure channels. Senders cache it and never use insecure channels until it expires. DANE for SMTP publishes a hash of the TLS certificate in DNS secured by DNSSEC. Real mail security lies in end-to-end methods on the message body, such as digital signatures.

sysd-q-129.title: Spam filtering
sysd-q-129.text: Spam filtering is an escalating game against people who keep inventing new evasions. It combines techniques that detect and refuse unsolicited bulk mail. They include content-based filtering, DNS-based blackhole lists (DNSBL), greylisting, spamtraps, enforcing SMTP's technical requirements and checksumming to detect bulk mail. Another is costs on the sender, such as proof-of-work or micropayments. Each has strengths and weaknesses. Bayesian filters rely roughly on word probabilities: a message with many words used only in spam and few never used in spam is likely spam. Machine learning more broadly can also identify spam. Spammers adapt, for example by adding random words to weaken Bayesian filters, which is called Bayesian poisoning. Outbound protection applies the same techniques to mail leaving a provider's network and blocks the message or shuts off its source. Email authentication against forged From addresses became popular in the 2010s, with servers using SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Filtering has collateral damage. It uses server and network resources. Rejected legitimate mail forces senders to contact recipients out of channel, and mail sent to a spam folder gives the sender no notice. Silently dropping mail violates the expectation that mail is delivered or returned, so it should be considered only with very high confidence that a message is seriously fraudulent. IMAP defines $Junk and $NotJunk keywords so users or delivery agents can mark junk, and $Phishing for likely phishing mail.

sysd-q-058.title: Designing Gmail
sysd-q-058.text:
Design the path that carries an email from one person to another. Alice sends from her client, and the Gmail server stores the mail and makes it available to Bob. SMTP's objective is to transfer mail reliably and efficiently, and email favors reliability over speed so it copes with unreliable network links and busy servers. RFC 5321 sets minimums: message content of at least 64K octets, 100 buffered recipients, local parts up to 64 octets and domains up to 255. Providers cap attachments, typically at 25MB or less in the early 2010s.

SMTP is the protocol between client and server and between mail servers, but it only delivers. The recipient's client fetches mail from the mailbox with IMAP or POP. A mail object is an envelope, with the error-return address and recipients, plus content of header and body. Delivery follows the envelope, so To can differ from the delivery list, and Bcc lives only in the envelope. Every message has a globally unique Message-ID, and replies name the parent in In-Reply-To and References, which lets a client rebuild conversation threads. Headers follow RFC 5322, and non-ASCII text and attachments use MIME.

The server keeps each mailbox: messages with strictly ascending UIDs and a UIDVALIDITY value, per-message flags such as \Seen and \Deleted, and folders. This server-held state costs far more per mailbox than POP.

Alice's client submits the message by SMTP to her mail server, on port 587 or 465 with authentication, and that server hands it to its mail transfer agent. The sending MTA asks DNS for the MX records of the recipient's domain and tries the lowest preference first, randomizing among equals. For a Gmail address the answer is Gmail's SMTP server. The MTA connects to the receiving server on port 25 and runs MAIL, RCPT and DATA, sending one copy for all recipients there. After the final 250 the receiver owns the message and must deliver it or report failure. A mail delivery agent saves the accepted message in the recipient's mailbox format, so the Gmail server holds the mail until Bob's client asks for it.

When Bob logs in, his client fetches new mail through the IMAP or POP server. IMAP leaves messages on the server so several clients share a mailbox, POP downloads and deletes, and IMAP IDLE pushes new-mail notices instead of polling. IMAP lets the server search so clients need not download every message, and fetch single MIME parts such as text without attachments. Searching massive mailboxes can overload the server unless storage, indexing and search are carefully built.

About 85% of email was estimated to be spam in 2021, so incoming mail is filtered by content, DNS blocklists, greylisting, Bayesian or learned models and sender authentication. Mail sent to a spam folder gives the sender no notice. Attachments travel as MIME parts. Original SMTP carries only 7-bit ASCII, so binary files are base64-encoded into a multipart message. The size the transport sees can differ from what the user sees. Mail that cannot be sent is queued and retried, at least 30 minutes apart, for at least 4-5 days. Several MX servers keep a domain accepting mail if one fails, and undeliverable mail is bounced with a null return path. The thing to remember is that the job splits in two: servers push mail with SMTP, and clients pull it with IMAP or POP.

openers.design-gmail: Sending an email looks like one act, but it is a relay race between programs. SMTP is the Internet standard protocol that mail servers and clients use to transmit electronic mail, and a message passes through user agents, submission agents, transfer agents and delivery agents, each with its own role. The message itself is a header section of fields followed by an optional body, and MIME extends the format to carry non-ASCII text and multimedia attachments. This chapter follows mail through the SMTP transaction, queues and retries, bounce messages and the MX record that names a domain's mail server. It ends with retrieval by POP and with spam, the unsolicited bulk mail that every mail design must handle.

reviews.design-gmail: The chapter follows one message end to end. SMTP carries it from the sender's client through submission and transfer servers, found with MX records, to the recipient's mailbox, and the envelope, not the header, decides where it goes. Queues, retries and bounce messages cover the cases where delivery fails, and security and spam filtering guard the path. POP and IMAP then let the recipient's client fetch the mail, with IMAP keeping state on the server through unique identifiers. The worked design joins these pieces: servers push mail with SMTP, and clients pull it with IMAP or POP.
